#4769. The BMW iX is sold out, but you might like what takes its place even more

BMW is saying goodbye to the iX. With the 2026 model essentially sold out, BMW is preparing to introduce its replacement, which already looks like a big upgrade.

The iX went on sale in the US in 2022 as BMW’s first dedicated electric SUV. After a short four-year run, BMW confirmed earlier this year that it was discontinuing the iX in the US after the 2026 model year to make room for its next-generation of fully electric vehicles.

BMW didn’t take long to sell through inventory, with 2026 iX models essentially sold out in the US.

The iX landing page now redirects you to the new BMW X5 instead. According to online auto research firm CarsDirect, about 10 new iX models remain nationwide.

BMW’s Neue Klasse vehicles, starting with the new 2027 iX3, mark a step change from its previous EVs.

At the center is the Neue Klasse platform, which introduces BMW’s sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive, new batteries, and an 800-volt electrical architecture.

BMW said the new Gen6 eDrive system delivers 30% higher charging speeds and driving range than its previous system, with some models seeing an even greater increase.

The 2027 iX3 50 xDrive, BMW’s first Neue Klasse vehicle, starts at $61,500 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 434 miles. In comparison, the 2026 iX xDrive 60 had an EPA range of up to 364 miles.

While the iX3 is a smaller, compact electric SUV compared to the iX, BMW is preparing to launch the iX5 as a more direct replacement.

The gas-powered 2027 X5 40 xDrive is now on sale, starting at $72,100, but BMW is expected to launch the electric iX5 in early 2027.

A few weeks ago, BMW put the new iX5 60 xDrive to the test at an international media event in Southern California to show just how fast it can charge.

During the event, the new iX5 hit a peak of 464 kW. BMW said that with up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes. To charge the battery from 10% to 80% takes just 22 minutes.

Using a 144 kWh battery, BMW said the electric SUV will offer up to an estimated 435 miles of range on a single charge.

The iX5 is powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, delivering a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW says it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 will be an upgrade from the iX, adopting BMW’s Neue Klasse design. The setup includes a 17.9″ navigation touchscreen and the new BMW Panoramic Vision that spans the windshield. You can also opt to add the optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.

The new drive platform is a huge improvement. Personally I'm glad to see it in the new i3 since I don't think everyone needs a 3-ton SUV.

Measuring 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, the iX5 is slightly longer and taller than the outgoing iX, with more of a traditional SUV design.

BMW is expected to open orders for the new iX5 60 xDrive this month, starting at $79,800, with a full launch in early 2027. It will be BMW’s first fully electric vehicle built in the US.

Production is set to begin at BMW’s Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina by the end of the year, with the first deliveries expected in early 2027.

#4767. What Does an Attention Deficit Really Mean?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Most of us have experienced what it’s like to struggle to pay attention to something. I’ll offer a recent example of my own.

My mind wandered further and further from the focus of the long academic meeting I was attending. I looked around at the others in the room. They seemed to be listening—or at least staring at the screen.

We were in a plush venue just off campus, the sort we often hire for these long meetings. Rain pounded on the glass roof. Beyond it, the grounds were lush and green.

A young waiter, about the same age as my son, clinked some glasses, replenished the water, juice and coffee, and left a tray of small chocolate brownies and fresh fruit at the back of the room.

I remember how I wanted one of the brownies and some plump green grapes, still shining with moisture. But walking to the back and helping myself felt rude. Everyone else seemed to be managing to pay attention. Weren’t they?

It felt as though I had lost all ability to focus.

But my attention hadn’t disappeared. I could focus on the rain, the trees, the grapes and the brownies. I could attend to them effortlessly. But I couldn’t keep my mind on the sixth presentation of the day.

I tried to care about what was being said. I really wanted to. But I simply couldn’t.

Something inside me had stopped cooperating. I’d reached a point of attentional saturation. It was a little like realising you’re full and that each extra mouthful feels forced.

I longed to get up, walk outside, or breathe fresh air. I wanted to think about something other than the presentation. I felt as though I was dying of boredom.

I felt resentful that I was expected to keep listening, but also guilty that I couldn’t find the attention the speaker seemed to deserve. What was wrong with me? Why was I so inconsiderate?

Perhaps you can remember similar experiences. Encountering situations in which our capacity to ‘pay attention’ is stretched is so often part of modern life.

I wondered what it reflected about me. Was I bored? Had the subject failed to interest me or feel important enough? Was it about motivation? Was I tired? Had I simply reached the limit of what I could sustain that day? Or was I reacting to an expectation that I should or must keep listening?

The idea that something can be ‘wrong’ with our ‘attention’ is now woven into the cultures and institutions in which we live. But psychologists don’t really use the term attention to describe one clearly defined ability.

In a 2019 paper, psychologists Bernhard Hommel and colleagues describe the common idea of attention as the mechanisms that help us make efficient use of our limited capacity to process, store and retrieve information. That sounds straightforward.

But the word is used as a proxy for a wide range of abilities and experiences:

These are all capacities that might be (and often are) referred to when someone uses the word ‘attention.’ However, Hommel and colleagues argue that it is highly unlikely that the same set of functional or neural mechanisms would be involved in and responsible for each of these. They also caution that dividing attention into neat, separate functions can obscure what those functions have in common too.

They’re all examples of "attention," but they might not share the same underpinning anatomical or neurological roots. This matters more than you might think. Their argument has implications beyond the lab.

For example, if attention describes different things, what are we saying when we tell someone to “pay attention”? Furthermore, what are we referring to when we say that someone has an “attention deficit”?

What’s more, when someone struggles to stay with a task, the difficulty may indeed involve attention. But it may also involve motivation, intention or emotion. Perhaps the task feels pointless, the person doesn’t want to do it, or they are bored. The label 'attention' alone doesn’t tell us which of these is at play in a situation.

Psychological labels deserve care and scrutiny, no matter how deeply entrenched they might be. A label can help us recognise a pattern. But it can frequently give us the impression that we understand more than we do.

The authors of the paper above ultimately concluded that we’d be better to drop the term 'attention' as a label for a specific functional or neural system, because, they argue, it doesn’t actually identify a single functional or neural system. This is significant.

If attention were no longer treated as the label for a single mental or neural system, what would we make of things like Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)? The name itself seems to point to a deficit in a particular capacity we call 'attention.' But if there is no single system called attention, then what, precisely, is deficient in something like ADHD?

This doesn’t necessarily make ADHD imaginary, or the difficulties people experience less real. But it does make the label seem less like an explanation than it first appears. Perhaps it names a recognisable pattern of difficulty, while leaving the processes, circumstances and histories that give rise to it in any one person wide open.

Hommel, B., Chapman, C. S., Cisek, P., Neyedli, H. F., Song, J. H., & Welsh, T. N. (2019). No one knows what attention is. Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 81 (7), 2288-2303.

#4766. A bull and a male donkey’s sexual relationship turns heads

Published Nov 2, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Sex between two animals of the same sex is widespread. Over 1,000 animal species from nematode worms to penguins to cattle all dabble in same-sex interactions. But a relationship between a bull named Achille and a male donkey named Patrocolo is raising eyebrows. The pair lives on a plateau in Ethiopia, and both could have chosen partners of the opposite sex and same species on numerous occasions. However, they continued to choose each other, despite belonging to different owners and only seeing one another when spending time in a pasture. A study published today in the journal Current Biology chronicles this surprising union.

“The sexual interactions between Achille, the bull, and Patroclo, the male donkey, were not isolated events,” Elisabetta Palagi, a study co-author and evolutionary biologist at the Università di Pisa (UNIPI) in Italy, said in a statement. “What really caught our attention was that these interactions were embedded in a very selective and consistent social relationship between the two individuals.”

The team first spotted these interactions while conducting another study earlier this year. They saw Achille mounting Patroclo, and were surprised to see that Patroclo did not try to avoid the bull, kick him, or show any defensive reactions.

“They repeatedly chose to stay close to each other and engaged in many different affiliative behaviors, such as licking, rubbing, and nuzzling, alongside the repeated mounting behavior,” added co-author André da Cruz, a PhD student at UNIPI. “Importantly, this was happening in a social environment where both animals had access to other potential partners, including individuals of both sexes and of their own species.”

The team recorded all of the interactions they witnessed involving either Achille or Patroclo. In total, the observed 51 mountings between the male bull and donkey from March 6 to March 19. In these interactions, Patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and then nipped at the bull. They repeatedly directed most of their sexual and social interactions toward each other, and the team reported no indication from the bull or donkey that either wished to discourage those advances. Achille mounted another male donkey only twice, and that other male showed avoidance behaviors and threatening expressions, like flattened ears.

“We believe the key finding is not simply that a bull mounted a male donkey,” said study co-author Martina Francesconi, also a PhD student at UNIPI. “It is that this unusual sexual behavior was part of a broader, selective social relationship. Our observations suggest that it cannot be easily explained simply by a lack of alternative mating opportunities, although we cannot say from this study exactly what function these sexual interactions may have had.”

According to the team, these observations have wider implications for our understanding of how sexual behavior is a complex social trait that goes beyond its role in reproduction. It also raises important questions for future studies, including if these interactions are primarily related to social bonding, what the benefits are, and if they play a role in reducing tension or maintaining relationships. In previous studies, same-sex mounting in nonhuman primates appears to be a form of conflict resolution and way to strengthen bonds, and may help male macaques reproduce more successfully.

“More broadly, we would like to better understand how social relationships shape sexual behavior and how behavioral flexibility allows animals to navigate complex social environments,” said Palagi. “We see this study as a starting point for asking these broader questions.”

#4765. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

The researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she said.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion said that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

#4761. Aloe found in ancient Egyptian mummy skull

Published Nov 2, 2026 12:58 PM EST

Archaeologists have identified a previously undocumented ingredient used in ancient Egyptian mummifications—and a famous medieval medicine concocted from the mummies themselves. At Germany’s Marburg University, researchers pinpointed traces of aloe-associated plant material in a 2,700-year-old mummy skull, and a popular centuries’ old apothecary cure-all known as Mumia vera aegyptiaca.

There is no one way to make a mummy. Mummification methods have varied across the world for thousands of years, even within a single culture. Ancient Egyptians honed their own processes over generations, and archaeologists are still sifting through millennia’s worth of artifacts and texts to better understand the iconic postmortem procedures.

Egyptology first truly took off in Europe during the late 18th century, but people’s fascination with mummies goes much further back in time. However, the long and complex medicinal history of mummy-derived treatments collectively called Mumia likely began as a 12th century mistranslation. Persian pharmacists often used a black pitch called mumiya in wound care, which medieval translators of Latin later mistook for similarly dark materials used in Egyptian mummification. This eventually led to an entire trade network centered on the import of powdered mummy remains sold by apothecaries as a Mumia cure-all—and sometimes even an aphrodisiac—for centuries.

Archaeologists have already documented many mummification ingredients derived from various minerals, animals, and plants. These span a range of coniferous tars and reins, oils, fats, beeswax, and bitumen, as well as rarer regional plant distillations like dammar and elemi. Knowing there is still much more to learn, the team at Marburg University recently analyzed 24 historically related objects stored at various institutions. These included an Egyptian mummified skull dated to the 8th century BCE, as well as an 18th century historical preparation of Mumia housed at Heidelberg Pharmacy Museum.

Their findings were recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and offer the first molecular evidence of mummy-related materials directly derived from aloe. This is particularly important, since “aloe” often historically referred to a variety of plants like agarwood outside the Aloe genus. According to Tanja Pommerening, a study co-author and director of Marburg University’s Institute for the History of Pharmacy and Medicine, the detection of aloe in Mumia is also particularly significant. Prior to this study, many researchers assumed medieval authors drew their Mumia recipes from biblical passages. These include John 19:39, which references a “mixture of myrrh and aloes.”

“The new findings suggest that this association may have deeper historical roots,” explained Pommerening.

However, since only two of the 24 artifacts in the study yielded traces of aloe, the frequency of the plant’s use in mummification and Mumia remains unclear. It’s possible that preparers may have only incorporated the material during certain historical periods, or depending on its availability. Still, Pommerening and her colleagues plan to continue similar examinations of other historical objects.

“Our goal is not only to analyze the chemical composition of ancient medicines and embalming materials, but also to gain a deeper understanding of their production, use, historical transmission, and cultural context,” added study co-author and Marburg University biologist Raphael Reher.

#4760. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4759. Life Is Not a Competitive Sport

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

We have all fallen into the comparison game at some point. Someone shares pictures from their exotic international trip. Someone else shares a professional achievement on LinkedIn. Yet another shares photos of their picture-perfect family. Whether these posts share the full story is a topic for another day, but the underlying commonality is how they can make us feel: like we will never be good enough or are somehow falling behind.

There is an excellent book by Rosamund and Benjamin Zander, The Art of Possibility, which touches on these themes. In it, the Zanders discuss what they call "the measurement world", describing how we all evaluate, compare, rank, and assign value to ourselves and others based on the variables that are most important to us. Their suggested antidote to this problem is to consider how one can uniquely contribute to the world around them without getting caught up in the comparison game.

They quote Martha Graham as told to Agnes DeMille to illustrate this idea:

“There is a vitality, a life force, a quickening that is translated through you into action, and because there is only one of you in all time. This expression is unique. And if you block it, it will never exist through any other medium and be lost. The world will not have it.

It is not your business to determine how good it is, nor how valuable it is, nor how it compares with other expressions. It is your business to keep it yours clearly and directly, to keep the channel open. You do not even have to believe in yourself or your work. You have to keep open and aware directly to the urges that motivate you. Keep the channel open" (as cited in Zander & Zander, 2000, p. 116).

The daily practice of humility can help us identify how we can be a unique and positive contribution to the world around us. Researchers have called humility "the just right view of the self," meaning you can identify both your strengths and weaknesses without feeling conceited or ashamed of them (Davis et al., 2016, p. 192). This prevents ego defensiveness and enables individuals to put their strengths to use and to recognize and encourage others' strengths without feeling threatened by them (Owens et al., 2013). Essentially, there is no need to compare ourselves to others, because we all have unique contributions to make.

While competition may be healthy in certain contexts, the continual ranking of ourselves against others is ultimately dysfunctional and detrimental to our own success. We can, however, learn from those we admire and aspire to be like. For example, replacing comparison with curiosity can prompt us to learn more about others in order to improve ourselves. Instead of feeling inferior or jealous, try coming up with a question you'd like to ask another person about their success, achievement, or good fortune. This also helps you see the context and effort behind their success and reduces the notion that their achievements can only be attributed to who they are.

The next time someone else’s success leaves you feeling behind, try the following steps:

This approach allows someone else’s success to become an opportunity for inspiration and perspective-taking, rather than a verdict on your progress and worth.

It's difficult to avoid everyone's highlight reel on social media: a promotion, an accomplishment, a milestone, a once-in-a-lifetime trip, but start to notice whether their good fortune automatically becomes a judgment about your own progress. Humility prompts us to recognize that we don't know everything and that we see only part of the story. We can appreciate what others have accomplished while continuing to pursue a life grounded in our own values. Someone else’s success does not have to become the measure of our worth.

Davis, D. E., Hook, J. N., DeBlaere, C., & Placeres, V. (2016). Humility at work. In L. G. Oades, M. F. Steger, A. Delle Fave, & J. Passmore (Eds.), The Wiley Blackwell handbook of the psychology of positivity and strengths-based approaches at work (pp. 191–209). Wiley. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118977620.ch12

Owens, B. P., Johnson, M. D., & Mitchell, T. R. (2013). Expressed humility in organizations: Implications for performance, teams, and leadership. Organization Science, 24(5), 1517–1538. https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.1120.0795

Zander, R. S., & Zander, B. (2000). The art of possibility: Transforming professional and personal life. Harvard Business School Press.

Yamaha is expanding its electric two-wheeler lineup with a much more capable machine, unveiling the new NMAX E as an electric version of its popular NMAX sport scooter.

The 2027 Yamaha NMAX E is being positioned as a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter, putting it firmly above the low-speed urban electric scooters that have made up much of Yamaha’s electric lineup thus far.

At its heart is Yamaha’s new compact eAxle drive unit, which sends power to the rear wheel through a belt drive. The electric motor produces 6.7 kW (9 hp) of nominal power and peaks at 7.5 kW (10 hp), along with 33.3 Nm (24.6 lb-ft) of torque.

Yamaha hasn’t published a top speed in the specifications, but the NMAX E’s A1 classification puts it in the same general category as 125cc combustion scooters rather than urban mopeds.

Power comes from a centrally mounted 3.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, which Yamaha says provides up to 104 km (65 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 testing cycle. The L-shaped battery is mounted low and centrally in the chassis to help maintain a low center of gravity.

Unlike many electric scooters that rely on removable batteries, the NMAX E uses a fixed pack. Yamaha has compensated for that with an onboard 800W charger, allowing riders to plug the scooter directly into a household outlet or an AC Type 2 public charging station. A full 0-100% charge takes around 5.5 hours.

Riders can choose between three riding modes. Sport (S) mode offers the quickest acceleration, Touring (T) provides smoother power delivery for everyday riding and carrying a passenger, and Eco (E) reduces acceleration and top speed while maximizing range. Regenerative braking is also included.

The rest of the scooter is fairly well equipped, including traction control, ABS, 245mm front and rear disc brakes, 13-inch wheels, a 33mm fork, dual rear shocks, and even a reverse mode to make low-speed maneuvering easier.

Nice, the Nmax has always been the premium scoot we try to get when traveling in southeast asia. Always felt like it would've been even better electrified. No removable battery seems a bit of a miss. That might constrain a big chunk of demand.

A five-inch TFT display includes smartphone connectivity through Yamaha’s Motor On app, providing turn-by-turn navigation as well as battery status, ride information, maintenance reminders, and other connected features. There’s also keyless ignition, USB-C charging, LED lighting, and illuminated underseat storage large enough for a full-face helmet, depending on its size.

Perhaps most importantly, the NMAX E looks like a proper Yamaha scooter rather than an electric experiment. Its dual headlights and distinctive side panels closely follow the styling language of Yamaha’s existing MAX family.

That could prove important as established motorcycle manufacturers increasingly attempt to bring electric models into their existing lineups rather than treating them as separate curiosities.

Pricing and exact market availability haven’t yet been announced, but Yamaha is positioning the NMAX E as a 2027 model for the European market.

#4756. Dinosaur blood found in fossils for the first time

Published Nov 2, 2026 3:00 PM EST

Paleontologists regularly discover fossilized dinosaur bones, but they sometimes locate footprints and prehistoric shells. On rare occasions, researchers have even identified the ancient indentations of a dinosaur’s skin or feathers. But fossilized cells? Researchers have long assumed such microscopic levels of preservation were impossible. But, once again, nature has proven otherwise.

In a study published today in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), an international team of paleontologists confirmed the presence of intact biomolecules and mineralized red blood cells inside fossils of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur. Although previous work has suggested similar possibilities, the team’s research is the first to chemically identify oxygen-carrying blood compounds known as heme.

“This really is a landmark discovery,” Kliti Grice, a study co-author and chemist at Curtin University in Australia, said in a statement. “These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time.”

The evidence exists inside the fossilized limb bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali. Discovered in 2008, A. museunacionali was an Early Cretaceous theropod that lived in present-day northeastern Brazil. The fossils suggest a dinosaur measuring over 10 feet long and weighing about 75 pounds, but given its young age, A. museunacionali likely grew even larger.

After carefully examining thin slices of the fossils, paleontologists located the mineralized red blood cell molecular components, along with a complex manganese oxide called hausmannite. This material helped maintain the cellular structures of heme, a ring-shaped molecule that contains iron and binds many proteins, especially hemoglobin. The hausmannite also helped preserve additional biomolecules found in the blood, such as the amino acids in collagen. The study’s authors theorize this level of preservation could only occur following a rapid burial in an environment that was rich in microbes, but low in oxygen at the same time.

Grice and her collaborators said that their discovery has wider implications for molecular-level paleontology. Further study could help advance our understanding of blood’s evolution, dinosaur metabolism, and ancient animals’ activity levels. The knowledge that this type of preservation is possible at all could even extend far beyond Earth. If such delicate biomolecules fossilize over millions of years in harsh environments, then it’s possible similar traces of life may linger elsewhere in the universe.

#4754. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. AWS provides scalable computing, automated software delivery, and advanced data analytics, including real-time construction intelligence, enabling Maximo to collect operational robotics data and continuously improve performance.

The rapid deployment of solar panels at utility scale projects like this one, which is set to eventually reach over a GW of solar generating capacity, will help companies like Amazon reduce their carbon footprint, of course – but also save them big money as the price of fossil fuels continues to climb.

So Primoris’ Renewables is the name of a business, Maximo is the name of a solar robotics company incubated by The AES Corporation. Maximo makes a robot (also called Maximo I think) using NVDIVIA hardware and software, and also AWS cloud software, and Bellefield is a solar field owned by Amazon. Or so I gather so far.

The Maximo team says it has plans to extend its robots potential use cases beyond solar and into construction tasks that require similar pick and place and feeding and attaching movements, site logistics, and site cleanup. And like just about every other business that demands a high degree of physical labor, the construction industry is facing huge labor shortages, making machines like Maximo that provide real efficiency gains welcome additions to the job site.

Optical cavities are pairs of light-trapping mirrors and underpin the operation of lasers, atomic clocks and many types of precision sensors. #4751. Ted Lasso’s Leadership Lessons in Emotional Intelligence

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Ted Lasso, the fictional expatriate manager of a floundering British association football (soccer…) team, is not in Kansas anymore. In the TV series that shares his name, his character tries earnestly to find his way as he helps others find theirs.

In a new country, in a new sport, in the ongoing tests of his crumbled marriage, Ted Lasso feels emotionally and culturally adrift. Yet flexibility fortifies him. So do curiosity, empathy, resolve, optimism, wit, and hope. At their lowest moments, he says to his team, “I believe in hope.” He hangs a hand-lettered sign over the team office door that says “BELIEVE.”

The character delivers wise soliloquies in affable Great-Plains cadences—to his discombobulated players, to his zany colleagues, and to his madcap bosses—without mixing a metaphor or resorting to cliché. (If you want platitudes or runaway similes, help yourself to NFL commentators at halftime.) You will not hear him say “when the going gets tough, the tough get going,” because he knows it’s all tough enough, even when it’s funny and heartwarming.

It is hard to remember having had more fun with background research than with this “Play in Mind” piece. And that is because, for starters, he approaches problem-solving as play.

When his team finds itself at sixes and sevens with performance anxiety, he orchestrates a pillow fight to relieve the tension that holds these grown men back.

When Sir Rupert, majority team owner, persistently rubbishes him at a pub, Ted Lures the aristocrat into a make-or-break darts contest bet by warming up with his clumsy right hand. And then, slyly remembering that he is left-handed, scores a winning bullseye while delivering a lecture about the value of curiosity. Judgmental people have everything figured out, he notes. But they fail to ask the key questions that would have averted their trouncing.

And then when a too-clever reporter asks this newcomer to explain the off-sides rule (note: nobody can clarify soccer’s murky off-side rule) he charms the press with a reference to American legal precedent: “I’m gonna put it the same way the U.S. Supreme Court put it back in 1964 when they defined pornography; it ain’t easy to explain but you know it when you see it.”

We also know playfulness when we hear it as the coach dispenses wisdom.

Here are samples of Ted Lasso’s best advice.

Be a goldfish. Forget the mistakes. In the first season, talented mid-fielder Sam Obisanya, insecure and homesick for his native Nigeria, despairs after a cocky teammate taunts him in practice. Ted, in his down-home way, urges him to drop the weight and move on. A goldfish is the happiest animal on earth, he says. Why? “got a ten-second memory.” “Be a goldfish, Sam.”

Turn “Me” into “Us.” Be a team player. The team’s striker and its most talented member presents the coach with a problem to solve. Jamie Tartt (rhymes with dart and tart) is the kind of player we used to call a hot dog or a showboat. Tactically, he frustrates play by hogging the ball. Strategically, his taunts cause friction. The coach appeals to the star player’s ambition by explaining that a truly great player needs to elevate those he plays with. Lasso’s gentle diagnosis implies a prescription. “I think that you are so convinced that you’re one in a million,” he says, “that you sometimes forget that out there, you’re just one of eleven.”

Do the Rightest Thing. When Sam Obisanya bravely duck-tapes over the name of the team’s sponsor that appears on his jersey, team owners shift to crisis mode. (That sponsoring company has caused environmental catastrophe in Sam’s native Nigeria.) Publicly resisting the greenwashing entails career risk. But Ted, the confident manager, reassures Sam: “doing the right thing,” he says, “is never the wrong thing.” As teammates also mask the logo in protest and sympathy, Sam begins to grow into a natural leadership role.

Play Through Him Not To Him. Ted leaves it to his Zen master of an assistant coach, Coach Beard, to articulate his vision of “total football.” In that strategy (more a philosophy) players are “no longer in set positions,” “defenders are free to attack.” And attackers are free to defend. It is about “letting go of your baggage and trusting your intuition.” The team uses its star player to draw the opponent out of balance, leaving him to pass the ball to a teammate in scoring position. It’s teamwork. “It’s jazz,” the philosophizer says.

Late in the series, Ted Lasso meets his match in the person of Dr. Sharon Fieldstone, the team’s new consulting professional sports psychologist, a no-nonsense Barbadian Londoner. She is summoned when a player suffers from “the yips,” a post-traumatic symptom that Ted’s humorous deflections cannot remedy.

When welcomed aboard with a ritual raucous cheer, she keeps a professional distance. When he calls her “Doc,” she corrects his familiar address. She is immune to the inspirational quotation.

Dr. Sharon Fieldstone, solid as a rock, represents a challenge to his everyday supportive, funny, folksy manner, the management style that works most days to distract players from their funk, but not every day — not with deep trauma. Having accidentally killed the team’s mascot, a greyhound, the player’s guilty turmoil cannot be chuckled away.

Here the series takes a thoughtful turn, saving the characters from caricature. Ted predictably resents the cross-disciplinary intrusion, of course, saying out loud that therapy is “bullsh*t.” He defends himself not merely because she is invading his turf.

Here is the crux: He resists the revelation that his jokey way conceals his own deep turmoil—unresolved grief, panic attacks, painful divorce, and family separation that are keeping emotional score. As with his total football strategy, he must move through obstacles resiliently before moving past them. Emotional life does not have a ten-second memory. The coach has his own growing to do. Optimism must be tempered with realism.

The therapist nails it for Ted with a basic, near-folksy therapeutic adage of her own. “The truth will set you free,” she observes pointedly, “but first it will piss you off.”

Bessel van der Kolk, The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, and Body in the Healing of Trauma (2014)

Stuart Brown, Play: How it Shapes the Brain. Opens the Imagination, and Invigorates the Soul (2011).

#4750. Watchful mama bear Gemini wins 2026 Helicopter Mom Award

Published Nov 2, 2026 4:07 PM EST

Even bears can be helicopter parents. The term coined in the 1990s by child development researchers Foster Cline and Jim Fay describes overly cautious parents who constantly monitor, control, and hover over (like a helicopter) their children’s activities out of fear.

For these watchful tendencies, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska has awarded a brown bear (Ursus arctos) named Gemini with the 2026 Helicopter Mom Award.

“We understand her choice, weighing the dangers of being around other bears at a prime fishing location,” the rangers write. “Still, we hope we see a lot more of them next year.”

The numbers also back up Gemini and other mother bears’ watchfulness. Brown bear cubs in Alaska have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent depending on the location. Gemini has also had cubs in 2023 and 2024.

The Rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The vast area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Like their beefy counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here exhibits their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4749. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4748. Do you need a preventative rabies vaccine? Probably not.

Published Nov 3, 2026 8:07 AM EST

Of all the deadly diseases that can spread from mammals to humans, rabies is the most infamous. Cujo had it. Old Yeller had it. A squirrel in “National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation” had it. Unfortunately, this virus doesn’t only live in fiction. It kills at least 59,000 people a year and is present in over 150 countries. On that list is the U.S., which is seeing a nationwide surge in reported cases of human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals.

If left untreated, rabies is always fatal (both for animals and humans). On the bright side, it’s also 100 percent preventable. Typically, in the U.S., humans get vaccinated for rabies after suspected rabies exposure, but right now many of us are wondering: Can and should you get vaccinated against rabies just as a precaution? Is there any benefit in getting a preventative rabies vaccine? The simple answer is no. Getting a pre-exposure vaccine doesn’t protect you from contracting the disease, and if you have an encounter with an animal that might have rabies, you’ll still need to get follow up doses regardless.

Before diving in, let’s clear up some common misconceptions about rabies and the rabies vaccine. Rabies is a zoonotic virus that comes in two types: furious rabies and paralytic rabies. Both types of rabies attack the central nervous system and both are fatal. Any mammal can be infected with rabies, and if infected, can transmit it to other animals or humans through a bite or scratch—even if you can’t see or feel the wound. Though rabies doesn’t turn its victims into people-eating zombies, as Hollywood would have us believe, it does deliver an acutely agonizing death.

The modern vaccine for rabies is made from cell culture. A cell culture vaccine contains no live virus. It is literally impossible for you to get rabies from the vaccine, which, you may be surprised to hear, is also pretty painless.

“The rabies vaccine is no more painful than a flu shot,” Dr. Edward R. Rensimer, a board-certified doctor of infectious diseases and internal medicine and director of the International Medicine Center in Houston, tells Popular Science.

If exposed to a rabid or possibly rabid animal, you will require more than one dose of a rabies vaccine.

“The injection site and number of doses recommended are dependent on the type of exposure you’ve had to a potentially rabid animal,” says Dr. Mirava Yuson, an epidemiologist and postdoctoral researcher working at the UCLA TIDE (Translational Infectious Disease Eco-epidemiology) Lab.

“You can expect, for example, that a bite wound induced by an animal that’s suspected to be rabid, versus a light scratch from an animal that is not suspected to have rabies, will merit different doses and numbers of recommended boosters that are needed to complete a vaccine series.”

Both Yuson and Rensimer cannot overstate the safety and efficacy of the rabies vaccine and emphasize that side effects, should they occur, are minimal.

“It is analogous to the flu vaccine,” Rensimer says, adding that in his more than 45 years of administering the vaccine he’s never seen a major adverse event.

“A very small minority of people in the 24 hours after the first dose may have low-grade fever, body aches, and malaise.”

So, the rabies vaccine is a totally safe, 100 percent effective, and generally gentle vaccine? Sign us up! In all seriousness, why wouldn’t we get this vaccine, regardless of exposure risk, especially now, when rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events are on the rise across the U.S.? Turns out there are a couple reasons why getting the rabies vaccine without any known risk exposure doesn’t make sense.

First, the “better safe than sorry” approach doesn’t work with rabies. Getting a rabies shot before a risk exposure event does not prevent you from becoming infected with rabies, nor does it minimize the effects of the fatal virus should you get it. You will still die if untreated by vaccinations post-exposure.

“There is a pre-exposure rabies vaccine that people get before traveling to rabies-endemic areas; however, the problem is, even if you get it, the minute you are exposed to a potentially rabid animal, you need a second dose, the post-exposure vaccine,” Yuson says.

“Veterinary professionals like me get them every year, but that does not preclude us from needing a post-exposure dose should we be potentially exposed. One vaccine is never enough and that is supremely important to know.”

Inside the school where dogs learn to sniff out bed bugs and other pests

Why do dogs’ legs shake during pets? It’s not because they like it.

Could a whale really swallow a human? We asked a biologist.

Second, getting a rabies vaccine regardless of risk exposure could confuse your case for clinicians if you do eventually face potential risk exposure.

“Getting the vaccine without known risk exposure can unfortunately cause some issues with the next dose should you be exposed or possibly exposed to a rabid animal,” Yuson says. “It becomes a question [for doctors]: ‘Do we start the regimen all over?’”

The best way to stay safe is also a bit of a bummer: It’s to limit contact with wildlife. All mammals are capable of getting infected with and transmitting rabies. In the U.S., there are infected raccoons, foxes, skunks and, most of all, bats, which are responsible for 70 percent of rabies deaths in people.

“The thing with bats, without getting too technical, is that they’re the only flying mammals,” Yuson says. “They can transmit diseases over great distances and can carry multiple diseases without themselves being sick, and they have very small fangs. You may not even feel the bite or often won’t see a bite wound.”

Because you may not even know you were bitten, it’s imperative that, after any encounter with a bat or any other potentially rabid creature, you immediately go to the ER and get the first of what will likely be a few post-exposure vaccines.

The vaccine is literally the only way to survive if you’ve been infected. There is no “wait and see” window, either.

“Once symptoms manifest, there is no cure for rabies; it has a 100 percent mortality rate and the only way to prevent infection after exposure is through vaccination,” Yuson says.

It’s a scary time, and rabies is a very scary virus, but remember that even with the spike in reported cases of human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals, a human dying from rabies is, in the U.S. at least, an incredibly rare thing.

“We average one to six cases of rabies a year in the U.S.,” Rensimer says.

Unfortunately, because of rising temperatures (rabies loves warm weather) and continued encroachment on wildlife habitats by good old mankind (leads to increased exposure risk among humans and pets), rabies doesn’t look to be going anywhere anytime soon.

But thanks to science, there’s no real reason to worry, because if for any reason we do come into contact with a possibly rabid animal, there’s a safe, accessible, and 100 percent effective vaccine available.

#4747. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4746. Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle

If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.

ReBake Motors has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.

Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.

Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.

There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.

The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.

Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.

The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.

Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.

CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.

ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.
